meanings.note: Prefix 'от-' ('away from, off') marks separation, completion, or response (stem 'куда').

examples.trans: Where does that word come from?
Thief, thief. Where does that word come from?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'here', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.
Common masculine noun meaning 'a boy cat, tomcat' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Well, the cat has smelled the cream.

examples.text: Держите. Только это не Матильда, это же кот!
examples.trans: Here you go. Only this isn't Matilda, it's a boy cat!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'he; it', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.
High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'a little; nearly', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Садись, не бойся. Я ведь сам чуть тебя не отпустил.
examples.trans: Sit down, don't be afraid. I very nearly let you go myself.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'not', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.
Prefix 'рас-' ('apart, un-, thoroughly') indicates distribution or intensive action (stem 'терзать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to tear to pieces'.

related.gloss: to to tear to pieces (prefixed perfective)
not to to tear to pieces (negated infinitive)

examples.trans: It was nearly torn apart by stray dogs.

examples.text: На кухне никто не хочет растерзать без причины.
examples.trans: In the kitchen nobody wants to tear to pieces without a reason.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'обака'). Common feminine noun meaning 'dog' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Я гуляю с собакой в парке.
examples.trans: I'm walking the dog in the park.

examples.text: Простите, это собака дочери. Я с ней гуляю пока.
examples.trans: Sorry, it's my daughter's dog. I'm walking her for now.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'all right, OK', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: All right, here you go. There, look.

meanings.note: Prefix 'от-' ('away from, off') marks separation, completion, or response (stem 'нести'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to carry to, take to', paired with 'относить'.

examples.text: Я сам отнесу блюдо в зал.
examples.trans: I will carry the dish into the dining room myself.
Take the documents to the boss.

examples.text: Я сейчас сам отнесу в зал.
examples.trans: I will carry it to the hall myself right now.

meanings.note: Prefix 'об-' ('around, about') marks encirclement or comprehensive action (stem 'ратно'). Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.trans: Afterwards I'll drive you back for free.

examples.text: Вот это дело! Потом обратно бесплатно отвезу.
examples.trans: Now we're talking! Afterwards I'll drive you back for free.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'on, onto; for', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: The programme is on the website.
He is running for a second term.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'мойка'). Common feminine noun meaning 'dumpster, trash heap, rubbish dump' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Take the bag to the trash dump.

examples.text: Ладно, я отнесу её на помойку.
examples.trans: Okay, I will take it to the dumpster.
He found a box in the dumpster.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'yes, indeed', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.
High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'to you', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?
And this is for you. A toy car!

examples.text: У тебя же есть ещё. Дай хоть одну.
examples.trans: But you've still got some. Give me just one.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning '(emphasis) after all, but', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: У тебя же есть ещё. Дай хоть одну.
examples.trans: But you've still got some. Give me just one.

meanings.note: Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('healthy; (colloq.) huge').

examples.text: Тихо, вы правы. Да, я здоров.
examples.trans: Quiet, you're right. Yes, I'm healthy.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'well; come on', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Ну что, очкарик? Видишь, ничего не осталось.
examples.trans: Well, four-eyes? See, there's nothing left.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to thank', paired with 'поблагодарить'.

examples.text: Всё, не благодари меня. И с Аникеевым реши.
examples.trans: That's it, don't thank me. And sort out Anikeev.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian clause-linking conjunction meaning 'if', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.
High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'what', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.

meanings.note: Prefix 'вы-' ('out of') marks outward movement or thorough completion (stem 'бросить'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to throw out, discard', paired with 'выбрасывать'.

examples.trans: He threw the mayor out the window.

examples.text: Он мэра в окно выбросил. Вы помните?
examples.trans: He threw the mayor out the window. Do you remember?

meanings.note: Formed with a diminutive/expressive Slavic suffix adding warmth or small scale. Common masculine noun meaning 'kitten' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Wait, did you throw the kitten out?

examples.text: На нашей кухне уже есть новый котёнок.
examples.trans: In our kitchen there is already a new kitten.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'in, into', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I grew up in a communal flat.
Hello! How was it in Hungary?

meanings.note: Derived noun with agent/object suffix '-ник'/'-щик'/'-чик'. Common feminine noun meaning 'hotel' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Ладно, поезжай в гостиницу, ты устала.
examples.trans: Alright, go to the hotel, you're tired.
We stayed at a small hotel.

examples.text: Ладно, поезжай в гостиницу, ты устала. Спасибо!
examples.trans: Alright, go to the hotel, you're tired. Thank you!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'for', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: We could open a salon for you.

examples.text: Для вас можно открыть салон красоты.
examples.trans: We could open a beauty salon for you.

meanings.note: Common neuter noun meaning 'animal' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Я добрый человек, я люблю животных.
examples.trans: I am a kind person, I love animals.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'let', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Ты преподавай. А они пусть строят свои торговые центры.
examples.trans: You teach. And let them build their shopping centres.

examples.text: А они пусть строят свои торговые центры.
examples.trans: And let them build their shopping centres.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian expressive spoken interjection meaning 'bye', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.
High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'there', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Hello! How was it in Hungary?

пожить.gloss: to live for a while, to stay

meanings.en: to live for a while, to stay
meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'жить'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to live for a while, to stay', paired with 'жить'.

examples.trans: You can stay at my place.

examples.text: Слушай, ты можешь пока пожить у меня.
examples.trans: Listen, you can stay at my place for now.

examples.text: Хочешь пожить у меня пару недель?
examples.trans: Want to stay at mine for a couple of weeks?

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'owner, proprietor, host' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: The restaurant owner personally greets the guests.
The owner is busy in the kitchen for now.

examples.text: Вовсе нет, я жду хозяина ресторана.
examples.trans: Not at all, I am waiting for the restaurant owner.

найтись.gloss: to be found, to turn up

meanings.en: to be found, to turn up
meanings.note: Prefix 'на-' marks surface contact, accumulation, or completing a quantity (stem 'йтись'). Reflexive/intransitive verb with the postfix '-ся'/'-сь' (historically from the reflexive pronoun 'себя', oneself). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to be found, to turn up', paired with 'находиться'.

examples.trans: Say thank you that the dog was found.

examples.text: Опоздал ты, Аркаша. Другие люди нашлись.
examples.trans: You're too late, Arkasha. Other people came along.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian clause-linking conjunction meaning 'and, but; so', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'at, by; (у меня) I have', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'I', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.
High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'such, like this', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.
Prefix 'у-' marks departure, removal, or successful completion (stem 'мничка'). Common feminine noun meaning 'clever one, good girl/boy' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Настя, ты у меня такая умничка.
examples.trans: Nastya, you are such a clever girl.

examples.text: На нашей кухне уже есть новая умничка.
examples.trans: In our kitchen there is already a new clever one.
